title: A Tool Built by Election Deniers Said These Voters Were Dead. We Found Them Alive.
author: Misty Harris
content:
Ahead of the midterms, conservative election activists discussed plans to
wield a powerful new weapon in the war against fraud: a data tool built by one
of their own that could identify suspicious voters and help with contesting
their ballots.

The system was put to the test this week in Forsyth County, Georgia, where a
member of the county’s election board provided other officials with what he
suggested was evidence of wrongdoing: four allegedly dead voters.

But it turns out all four are alive and well, ProPublica determined. The board
rejected the attempt to challenge their ballots.

The effort, though, shows that even after last week’s blue wave, those who
believe the 2020 election was stolen have continued to relentlessly search for
ways to contest Republican losses. In Georgia, Democrats [swept statewide
offices](https://georgiarecorder.com/2026/11/04/democrats-flip-statewide-
offices-up-and-down-the-ballot-in-georgia-state-house-is-in-play/).

The board member who initiated the Forsyth County challenge, Max Clavijo, is a
member of the Election Integrity Network, a group led by conservative lawyer
Cleta Mitchell that works to restrict voting and tighten election laws and
rules. Mitchell worked closely with Donald Trump in his attempt to overturn
his defeat in the 2020 election and, since he retook the presidency, has been
[central to his push to assert greater federal control over
voting](https://www.propublica.org/article/cleta-mitchell-elections-trump).

In the run-up to the midterms, on right-wing media and on private organizing
calls, EIN participants outlined plans to search voter rolls with a software
tool known as ELLY’s Election Monitor and contest ballots the tool deemed
suspicious.

ELLY was developed by EIN member Rick Richards. It aggregates public data from
state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents,
obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources. In Georgia, State
Election Board members and top staffers have urged counties to use the tool to
search their voter rolls for signs of fraud.

Richards talked about ELLY’s national potential on a podcast in late
September, on which right-wing media personalities and activists touted its
capacity to help [GOP candidates](https://rumble.com/v7g5kq4-election-
integrity-live-stream-with-steve-stern-sep.-30-2pm-est.html?start=708) contest
their defeats. “We can prove the fraud that’s gone on in every state,” one
commentator said. “This data will be able to set up challenges to those who
lose.”

The following month, on a private call with EIN members and other conservative
activists, Richards promised to provide data from more than 3,000 counties to
“citizen monitors” and GOP candidates to try to prove fraud, according to a
recording reviewed by ProPublica.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261027-cleta-
mitchell-today.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s
“Big Lie” Into a Movement** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/cleta-
mitchell-elections-trump)

In an interview, Richards told ProPublica that he gave Clavijo data on Forsyth
County at Clavijo’s request. He said in a subsequent email that their actions
were meant to inform the board and remain confidential. Clavijo didn’t respond
to questions from ProPublica.

Richards refused to answer questions about whether Clavijo’s effort was part
of a wider EIN campaign to contest votes cast in the midterms.

“That’s irrelevant,” he said. “The data is the data. People can use it for
what they want to.”

Mitchell, EIN’s leader, didn’t respond to questions about the group’s plans
related to ELLY, either in Georgia or nationally.

In the months since some on Georgia’s State Election Board started promoting
ELLY’s use, its accuracy has been much debated. The tool doesn’t have access
to personal identifiers such as voters’ Social Security or driver’s license
numbers or full dates of birth, which increases the potential for mismatches
involving people with the same names.

Voting rights groups have called ELLY [error-
prone](https://campaignlegal.org/sites/default/files/2026-08/Elly%20Backgrounder%20%28Aug%204%2C%202026%29.pdf).
The Cherokee County election director complained to the state board after the
[tool falsely flagged a county board member’s spouse as
dead](https://www.ajc.com/politics/2026/07/georgia-election-board-promotes-
new-voter-roll-tool-ahead-of-midterms/).

State Election Board members and Richards have defended ELLY. Accusations that
the data is unreliable were “horse hockey,” Richards told ProPublica,
explaining this was “a Southern colloquialism for B.S.”

Late last week, according to several people familiar with the matter, Clavijo
circulated documents to board members and Forsyth County’s election director.
Based on data from ELLY, Clavijo questioned whether the names of more than
22,000 people on the county’s voter roll were correct and disputed the
eligibility of 69 voters. In addition to four he claimed were deceased, he
alleged others had moved out of the county or state, had voter ID
irregularities or had registered under fictitious names, giving an initial as
their first name.

During the meeting, Clavijo claimed that he was not trying to disrupt the
election’s certification or formally challenge the voters, a process outlined
in statutes that can lead to ballots being tossed or voters removed from the
rolls. (Richards also said they had not formally challenged ballots.) Clavijo
said he was merely seeking “to clean the voter rolls” and inform the board so
officials could investigate further.

But other board members accused him of doing an end run around the formal
challenge process. Barbara Luth, the board chair, said she felt “sorry for”
Clavijo because activists were bypassing the challenge procedure “by coming to
you and having you submit it.”

Under fire from fellow board members, Clavijo admitted he could not vouch for
the data’s accuracy.

“I did not make any explicit accusation that the information was 100%
correct,” he said.

The cover letter Clavijo submitted with the challenges said that they had not
been verified with any “human review,” according to sources familiar with the
matter.

Richards and Clavijo submitted obituaries for the voters they claimed were
dead, but there were discrepancies between the information in them and the
voters’ records. All of the obituaries said or suggested the deceased lived
outside of Forsyth County, which would have made it impossible to vote there.
One said [the person lived in
Arizona](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/273568455/alexis-ramirez).

ProPublica confirmed that all four are actually alive.

Alexis Ramirez, a night-shift nurse, told ProPublica that she cast her ballot
during early voting. She was surprised to hear her vote had been contested —
and why.

“It’s kind of crazy that they attempted to do that without trying to prove it
first,” she said.

Saramma George, another voter Richards and Clavijo claimed was dead, said she
was “really angry” to have the validity of her ballot questioned.

In the third case, ProPublica spoke with a voter’s son, who said she was alive
but didn’t want to talk to ProPublica. Her “ballot is valid,” he said.

The fourth voter, Chris Strickland, said, “I don’t know where they’re getting
their information from, but it’s false. I’m alive. I’m here.”

The majority of the challenges — 38 of them, according to people familiar with
the matter — involved voters who’d registered using an initial.

One voter, Alexander Knight, told ProPublica that he goes by his middle name
and that the information in voter records mirrors how Department of Driver
Services officials suggested he be identified on his driver’s license.

“I am real,” he told ProPublica.

Four other challenged voters said they, too, abbreviated their first names. A.
Joseph Guntherberg confirmed he routinely used the same formulation of his
name, adding that blocking his ballot would not help the challengers: “My
candidate didn’t win.”

Richards said it was up to county election workers to check ELLY’s data — he
merely gathers it to facilitate efforts to maintain accurate voter lists.

But at the meeting, Joel Natt, a Republican board member, said the
responsibility lay with challengers to justify their accusations. “This has no
relevance to anybody here until” they provide solid evidence, he said,
“through the proper channel.”
